facts.text: Known hypersensitivity (including anaphylactic or serious skin reactions) to naproxen or any component of the product.
History of asthma, urticaria, or other allergic‑type reactions after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs (aspirin‑sensitive asthma).
Use in the setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.
NSAIDs, including naproxen, increase the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events (myocardial infarction, stroke) which may occur early in therapy and rise with duration and dose.
facts.population: All patients, especially those with existing cardiovascular disease or risk factors

facts.text: NSAIDs cause serious gastrointestinal adverse events (bleeding, ulceration, perforation) that can be fatal and may occur without warning symptoms. Risk is higher in elderly patients and those with prior peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding.
facts.population: Elderly patients and patients with prior ulcer/GI bleed

facts.text: Hepatotoxicity: elevations of ALT/AST ≥3× ULN in ~1% of patients; rare cases of fulminant hepatitis. Monitor liver enzymes and discontinue if signs of liver injury develop.
Hypertension: NSAIDs may blunt the antihypertensive effect of ACE inhibitors, thiazide or loop diuretics. Monitor blood pressure.
Heart failure and edema: avoid in severe heart failure unless benefit outweighs risk; monitor for worsening heart failure and consider sodium load (50 mg Na per 500 mg naproxen sodium tablet).

Renal toxicity: dose‑dependent reduction in renal prostaglandins may precipitate renal decompensation, especially in patients with impaired renal function, dehydration, hypovolemia, heart failure, liver disease, or those taking diuretics/ACE‑I/ARBs. Monitor renal function; avoid in advanced renal disease unless benefit outweighs risk.
facts.population: Patients with renal impairment, dehydration, heart failure, or on diuretics/ACE‑I/ARBs

facts.text: Hyperkalemia: NSAIDs can increase serum potassium, even in patients with normal renal function.
facts.population: All patients, especially those on potassium‑sparing agents

facts.text: Anaphylactic reactions: may occur in patients with or without known naproxen hypersensitivity; seek emergency care.
Serious skin reactions (SJS, TEN, exfoliative dermatitis, GBFDE) may be fatal; discontinue at first sign of rash or hypersensitivity.
Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS) reported; discontinue and evaluate immediately if suspected.

Fetal toxicity: avoid after ~30 weeks gestation due to risk of premature closure of ductus arteriosus; limit use between 20–30 weeks to lowest effective dose and shortest duration; monitor amniotic fluid if >48 h.

Hematologic toxicity: NSAIDs may cause anemia from occult/gross bleeding or affect erythropoiesis; monitor hemoglobin/hematocrit, especially with concomitant anticoagulants, antiplatelets, SSRIs, SNRIs.
facts.population: Patients with bleeding risk or on anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy

facts.text: Concurrent low‑dose aspirin increases risk of serious GI events.
NSAIDs may reduce efficacy of antihypertensives (ACE‑I, ARBs, thiazides, loop diuretics).
Avoid use of more than one NSAID simultaneously; naproxen-containing products should not be co‑administered.
Increased bleeding risk when combined with warfarin, other anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, SSRIs, or SNRIs.

Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration. Rheumatoid arthritis/osteoarthritis/ankylosing spondylitis: naproxen 250 mg (½ tablet) then 500 mg twice daily; naproxen sodium 275 mg (½ tablet) then 550 mg twice daily. Dose may be titrated up to 1500 mg/day for up to 6 months if needed.
Acute gout: start 750 mg naproxen tablets, then 250 mg every 8 h until attack resolves; naproxen sodium 825 mg start then 275 mg every 8 h.
Primary dysmenorrhea, acute tendonitis/bursitis, pain: start 550 mg naproxen sodium (tablet) then 550 mg q12 h or 275 mg q6‑8 h PRN; total daily dose ≤1375 mg initially, ≤1100 mg thereafter.
Polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis: total daily dose ≈10 mg/kg in two divided doses; naproxen tablets not appropriate for children <50 kg – consider liquid formulation.
Elderly patients have a greater risk of serious GI events and may be more susceptible to renal toxicity; monitor renal function and consider lower starting doses.

Long‑term NSAID use can cause papillary necrosis and worsen pre‑existing renal disease; correct volume status before initiating therapy; monitor renal function and serum potassium; avoid in advanced renal disease unless benefit outweighs risk.
facts.population: Patients with renal impairment or at risk (dehydration, heart failure, liver disease, elderly)
